I'll leave some translation notes for you to consider:
------------------------------------------------------------------
The "Nu" (奴) Naming Convention

Throughout this story, converted women receive new names formed by taking a fragment of their original names and appending 奴 (nú)—a Chinese character historically associated with slavery and servitude, and carrying connotations of submission. This produces names such as Reina → Nanu, Huilan → Huinu, and Ayana → Nainu.

While these names may initially appear to be simple aliases, their significance runs deeper. Each new name reflects the character's changed status and her place within the hierarchy she has entered.

By adopting the name willingly, their complete submission—the result of brainwashing and corruption—is laid bare for us to see.
The naming convention thus serves as another marker of their transformation—and of how deeply that transformation has come to shape their sense of self.
-------------------------------------------------------------------
Self-Referential Expressions

One of the most distinctive features of the original Chinese text is its frequent use of self-referential expressions—terms characters use to refer to themselves. Where English generally relies on “I” and “me,” Chinese offers a wider range of such expressions, each carrying its own connotations of status, hierarchy, intimacy, and submission—from the haughty 本小姐 (“this young lady”) to the self-abasing 贱奴 (“this lowly slave”).

While these expressions carry meaningful character and cultural nuances, reproducing them literally every time they appear can make English dialogue sound repetitive or unnatural. For this reason, the translation occasionally tones down explicit self-references, preserving them where they provide emphasis or are particularly important to a character's voice, while allowing their implications to come through in the surrounding wording, tone, and context elsewhere.

The aim is not to erase these distinctions, but to convey their effect in natural English.
--------------------------------------------------------------------
“Demon Star” vs. “Planet Demon”

Some of you may have noticed that in the earlier chapters, I used the term “Demon Star” before changing it to “Planet Demon.” This inconsistency was my mistake, and I only caught it later in the translation process.

The Chinese character 星 (xīng) can refer to a star or, depending on the context, a planet or other celestial body. In this story, the names of the primary inhabited worlds—地星 (Planet Earth) and 魔星 (Planet Demon)—both use this character. Since these worlds have their own populations, militaries, and governments, “Planet” is the more appropriate rendering in this context.

I've therefore standardized the terminology to use “Planet” consistently throughout the translation. This not only better reflects the worldbuilding but also maintains the internal consistency of the setting and reinforces the planetary scale of the conflict.
